title: The Cytator Strikes Back: Kara Peterson & Rich DiBona On Descrybe’s Fresh Take on Legal Research
author: Kara Peterson · Richard DiBona

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source does not directly endorse the cluster’s claim that automation weakens apprenticeship and partner-succession routes. Instead, it constructively reframes the organisational challenge around scarce transition talent and competition for implementation resources, especially at small and mid-sized firms; its claims about model capabilities remain task-specific and qualitative.
qs: And also just the pace of change means there’s talent shortage and it’s hard to hire people to come into your firm, especially if it’s a smaller firm or even a mid-sized firm and help you with these transitions because labor is scarce.
So I think we’re entering a rapidly increasing change with ⁓ some very serious competition for resources.

st.an: The source raises a tentative concern that advanced models and platforms may be commoditised or insufficiently differentiated, which is relevant to the cluster’s unresolved architecture question. st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, task-bounded deployment and adds a concrete implementation model: constrain AI to curated legal data, precompute analysis, retrieve stored results, and retain citation checking. This materially develops the cluster’s emphasis on task design, reliable data and verification, although its performance and adoption claims remain largely anecdotal.
qs: So the way we built our thing was just by giving concrete pieces of data and having the AI operate just on that thing.
So you need to check what you receive too.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value

st.an: The source supports the proposition that AI value depends on organisational capacity to manage change rather than technical capability alone. Peterson identifies legal-sector resistance to rapid innovation and scarce transition talent, particularly for smaller firms, while DiBona’s task-specific capability claims reinforce the distinction between model strength and successful institutional adoption. Its claims are forecasts and assessments, not measured adoption outcomes.

kp.k: AI enables citation analysis previously requiring extensive human editing
kp.d: DiBona attributes Descrybe’s development to AI accelerating the work of an already-skilled programmer and enabling case-treatment analysis that would otherwise require approximately a thousand human editors. Peterson argues that previously prohibitive human analysis costs limited these research capabilities. These are the developers’ explanations, not measured productivity or employment findings.
qs: if you already knew how to program really well, it could really kind of help accelerate things.
like analyzing for case treatments you couldn’t have done without AI because you needed, you know, thousand human editors.

kp.k: Precomputed analysis replaces live LLM calls during research
kp.d: DiBona says Descrybe performs its AI analysis upfront and subsequently queries stored results, displaying citation treatments directly within search results. He presents this architecture as enabling rapid navigation rather than repeated waits for model responses; the transcript provides illustrative latency comparisons rather than a formal performance test.
qs: when you make a request to Descrybe, we’re not calling an LLM and then giving you the results back from the LLM. We’ve, we did all that work upfront.
you see the citator treatments in every search result.
by the time it gets to the point of being in our platform, we’re basically doing database queries against previously generated stuff.

kp.k: Issue-level citation treatment supports more specific legal research
kp.d: DiBona reports analyzing close to 30 million citations and distinguishing treatment of individual issues rather than only whole cases. He says a citing decision may follow some issues while overruling another, leaving potentially usable propositions that whole-case indicators obscure. This is a description of product functionality and observed examples, without quantified accuracy results.
qs: what we did was just analyze, I think it’s close to 30 million citations to see what the treatment was.
we said what issues did it treat on and how did it treat those issues.
we found a lot of examples where it will follow on some issues and then overrule just on one particular issue.

kp.k: Backward citation analysis exposes decisions’ historical foundations
kp.d: DiBona describes the backward citator as showing which precedents judges cited and how they treated them, complementing later decisions’ treatment of the focal case. He suggests this may be particularly useful to researchers. Separately, host Gebauer proposes using it to trace doctrinal breaks and explain them in legal arguments.
qs: when the judges wrote the case, what cases did they cite and how did they treat them?
It might be more for researchers, but it was something that we thought was really cool. So we just decided to give it to everybody.
you can kind of see where breaks happened and then be able to explain, you know, in your argument why those, those breaks happened

kp.k: Citation ambiguity requires iterative testing and expert input
kp.d: Asked about accuracy and human validators, DiBona describes testing with legal-librarian and academic advisers, extensive trial and error, and comparing several advanced models on ambiguous examples. He identifies parenthetical citations as an error source: AI can assign overruling treatment to the wrong case. His account describes development practices, not systematic human verification of every result or a reported error rate.
qs: We actually have advisors who are legal librarians and people at university and most of them are academics. So we’ve done a lot of testing with them
it cites a case, but it’s really like a parenthetical for another case.
And I would do this against like several different models and say, like, what do think the treatment is?

kp.k: Constrained source processing aims to reduce hallucination risk
kp.d: DiBona says Descrybe constrains AI to supplied data rather than asking it to augment material, while Peterson argues the closed information set minimizes unexpected outputs. DiBona also describes a brief checker that identifies hallucinated citations and citation treatment, including in opposing counsel’s submissions. These are vendor safeguard and functionality claims, without measured hallucination rates.
qs: the way we built our thing was just by giving concrete pieces of data and having the AI operate just on that thing.
it does minimize the potential for really weird stuff to happen.

it’ll find hallucinated citations for you and also the treatment of them because even if you’re perfect in yours, you might receive one from the other attorney. So you need to check what you receive too.

kp.k: Low-cost professional tools complement continuing free search
kp.d: Peterson says Descrybe launched in summer 2023, retains free search, and added a professional legal research toolkit containing approximately 18 tools. She gives monthly prices of $10 for non-commercial use and $20 for commercial use, with users trusted to select the appropriate tier. The speakers position affordability as serving access to legal information and occasional professional research needs; DiBona’s account of lawyers unable to justify $500 monthly subscriptions is explicitly anecdotal.
qs: we launched in summer of 2023
we had a free search and we still do
it’s a collection of maybe 18 or so different tools
if you’re using it for non-commercial use, it’s 10 bucks a month. If you’re using it for commercials, 20 bucks a month
What we’ve heard anecdotally is that there’s a bunch of lawyers who they have a need for legal research, but they can’t justify paying for the $500 a month thing

kp.k: Reported adoption lacks granular usage attribution
kp.d: DiBona explicitly says he does not know which tools drive signups. Peterson links this limitation partly to avoiding detailed user tracking, reports rapidly increasing conversions, and attributes appeal to price, usability, speed and output quality based on feedback. Neither supplies signup counts, conversion rates or a systematic customer study.
qs: I’m actually not sure what is driving people, what tools specifically are driving people to sign up.
we also don’t track our users in the way like a lot of tools do.
people are converting like at a scale that’s like increasing really rapidly
It’s just how easy and intuitive and simple they are to use.

kp.k: Curriculum distribution expands exposure to affordable research tools
kp.d: Peterson reports a planned fall rollout into a National Society for Legal Technology curriculum reaching 350 schools, including law schools and paralegal programs. She describes its international reach with uncertainty as approximately 11 countries. She presents Descrybe as filling a curriculum space left by CaseText’s withdrawal of free search; this is a distribution announcement, not evidence of student learning outcomes.
qs: he had a space to fill in his curriculum that goes out to about 350 universities.
He does law schools and paralegal programs across the world. Actually, it’s like, I think, 11 countries.
we are officially rolling out this fall into a legal curriculum that’s again, in 350 schools.

kp.k: Expansion beyond case law retains cost-based pricing ambition
kp.d: DiBona reports work incorporating statutes, regulations, state constitutions, court rules, attorney general opinions and session laws, saying the process has covered the 10 biggest states. The intended functionality includes searching across jurisdictions and material types. He says the additional content is planned for inclusion without a price increase and contrasts cost-based pricing with charging whatever the market will bear.
qs: We’ve done like the 10 biggest States
statutes, regulations.
state constitutions, court rules, attorney general opinions
But session laws.
we don’t plan on charging any more for it. We’ll just include it.
based on cost rather than based on how much we can charge.

kp.k: Consolidation creates perceived openings for affordable research providers
kp.d: In response to Lambert’s discussion of CaseText and vLex acquisitions, Peterson sees continuing room for affordable providers and relates this to access to justice and open information. She reports journalist Bob Ambrogi’s assessment that Descrybe could fill the space CaseText is leaving; that assessment is relayed by the vendor. Her comparison with earlier providers explicitly leaves Descrybe’s eventual scale uncertain.
qs: we were poised to fill the space that CaseText is leaving in the market
the need is not gone. The need is still there.
you kind of can do the Fastcase CaseText Descrybe thread, right?
whether or not we end up, you know, anywhere near that scale, you know, TBD

kp.k: Curated data becomes strategically important to legal technology
kp.d: Peterson argues that clean, curated legal datasets are increasingly valuable both for access and for larger providers’ businesses. Gebauer emphasizes that poorly structured data limits advanced tools’ effectiveness, while Peterson warns of harmful outputs. DiBona suggests users’ expectations of comprehensive platforms pressure companies to acquire missing capabilities. Lambert separately speculates whether data demand could eventually attract Microsoft or OpenAI to acquire major legal-technology companies.
qs: this kind of clean data sets of really good curated case law and other things that Rich was mentioning before are really a hot commodity right now.
if they don’t have it structured and clean, then they, these wonderful, high tech tools are not as effective.
if you’re not getting the right outputs back, you’ve just set yourself back even further than if you didn’t have it in the first place.
there’s an expectation from users that you could just go to one place and get everything now.

kp.k: Accelerating change may intensify firms’ implementation talent constraints
kp.d: In the closing forecast, Peterson predicts unprecedented acceleration that will be especially difficult for a legal industry she characterizes as weak at rapid innovation. She anticipates scarce transition-support talent and competition for resources, particularly affecting smaller and mid-sized firms. This is a qualitative prediction rather than labor-market evidence.
qs: the pace of change is just going to continue to accelerate to an extent that we have never seen
quick change and rapid innovation is not necessarily, I would say, a core strength for many in the legal industry.
it’s hard to hire people to come into your firm, especially if it’s a smaller firm or even a mid-sized firm and help you with these transitions because labor is scarce.

kp.k: Stronger general models may commoditize specialized platform capabilities
kp.d: DiBona identifies commoditization as a forward-looking concern motivating continued product development. He describes GPT-5’s high-reasoning programming and analysis capabilities as powerful and questions how different direct use of advanced models will be from specialized platforms. He does not establish equivalence through comparative testing.
qs: the programming part and the analysis part is super powerful on this high reasoning.
So I think about things getting commoditized a bit
can you be sure that’s something that you put in to some of these advanced models? will be that much worse or different than what you put into some of these advanced platforms.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: DiBona claims AI makes small-team development of sophisticated legal research tools feasible and accelerates programming by experienced developers.
pts.d: At 34:05, Rich DiBona attributes Descrybe’s development to AI-assisted programming and automated case-treatment analysis that previously would have required a large human editorial workforce. This is a retrospective claim about production capacity, not a report of measured job displacement.

pts.k: DiBona claims precomputed AI analysis enables fast, issue-specific citation research and historical exploration.
pts.d: At 06:08–10:24, DiBona describes displaying treatments within search results, distinguishing treatment of individual issues rather than just whole cases, and showing how a decision treated earlier authorities through a backward citator. He says preprocessing avoids waiting for live LLM responses. Peterson qualifies the novelty claim by declining to assert that comparable features do not exist elsewhere.

pts.k: Peterson and DiBona position low-cost AI-enabled research as serving an affordability gap and plan to expand coverage without raising prices.
pts.d: At 12:21–23:01, the speakers describe a continuing free search product and a professional toolkit priced at $10 monthly for noncommercial use and $20 for commercial use. They identify unmet demand among occasional legal researchers and connect their offering to access to legal information. DiBona says planned coverage includes statutes, regulations, constitutions, court rules, attorney general opinions and session laws. These are product and market claims; the transcript does not establish improved civil justice outcomes.

pts.k: DiBona and Peterson claim constrained preprocessing reduces hallucination exposure, while their brief checker helps identify fabricated citations.
pts.d: At 28:46–30:21, DiBona says AI operates on concrete supplied data and users subsequently query previously generated material rather than trigger live generation. Peterson says this closed information environment minimizes anomalous outputs. DiBona also claims the brief checker finds hallucinated citations and reports citation treatment, including in opposing counsel’s submissions. No quantified hallucination rate or detection accuracy is supplied.

pts.k: Peterson claims curated legal data is increasingly commercially valuable and that poor data can make AI use harmful.
pts.d: At 23:01 and 26:49, Peterson links demand for curated case law and other legal information both to access to information and to the business needs of larger companies. She warns that complex datasets can produce misleading outputs when handled inadequately. These claims reflect her market impressions and reasoning rather than a quantified market study or documented harm cases.

pts.k: Peterson predicts accelerating change and competition for transition expertise; DiBona anticipates possible commoditization of specialized platforms.
pts.d: At 36:04, Peterson predicts unusually rapid change that will be especially difficult for a legal industry she views as poorly adapted to rapid innovation. She expects scarce talent to impede transitions, particularly at smaller and midsized firms. At 37:02, DiBona questions how much specialized platforms will differentiate themselves as advanced general-purpose models improve in programming and analysis. He presents commoditization as a concern, not an established equivalence between models and legal products.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Technical claims rest on the developers’ account of large-scale processing, iterative testing and expert advice, not reported independent performance benchmarks.
pts.d: At 03:56–05:09, DiBona describes analyzing approximately 30 million citations, working through attribution errors involving parentheticals, testing with academic and law-librarian advisers, and comparing model interpretations of ambiguous passages. The citation count describes processing scale, not measured accuracy. The transcript does not specify a validation protocol, error rate, benchmark score or independent comparison. The speakers’ development experience also supports their feasibility claims.

pts.k: Adoption and affordability claims rely on anecdotal feedback and unspecified conversion growth; forecasts are experiential judgments.
pts.d: At 14:01–15:26, DiBona explicitly says he does not know which tools drive signups. Peterson explains that limited user tracking constrains granular knowledge and attributes adoption to price, usability and output quality based on feedback. No signup totals, growth rates, comparative quality measures or labor-market statistics are provided. The acceleration, talent-scarcity and commoditization forecasts are not accompanied by formal studies.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source distinguishes existing capabilities in 2025 from a fall education rollout and an unfinished expansion of legal coverage.
pts.d: Peterson dates the original launch to summer 2023 and describes the free service and professional toolkit as available at the interview. She announces a fall 2025 rollout through a curriculum reaching approximately 350 schools, rather than reporting completed adoption by all those institutions. DiBona describes broader legal-source ingestion as underway, with approximately the ten largest states processed, but supplies no completion date. Inclusion without additional charges is a stated plan.

pts.k: Efficiency and reliability claims depend on experienced programming and constrained processing; future disruption has no precise deadline.
pts.d: DiBona qualifies programming acceleration by prior developer competence. The speed and hallucination-reduction claims concern a research system using precomputed material, not document generation or unrestricted live model responses. Peterson’s forecast concerns the coming months and years in a discussion referencing ten months and two years, but supplies no dated milestone. DiBona’s commoditization concern depends on advanced models narrowing meaningful differences from specialized platforms.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected users include occasional lawyer-researchers, professional researchers, educators and students, and lawyers checking submitted briefs.
pts.d: The speakers identify lawyers with intermittent research needs as beneficiaries of lower prices; researchers gain issue-specific and historical citation analysis. Peterson describes educational distribution to law schools and paralegal programs. DiBona emphasizes checking both one’s own briefs and material received from other attorneys. Their access mission concerns more affordable legal information, without evidence here that people with unmet civil legal needs obtain representation or better outcomes.

pts.k: Providers face changes in production economics, competitive differentiation and hiring needs.
pts.d: DiBona’s account concerns a legal-tech vendor building research software with less editorial labor than he believes historically necessary; it is not an ALSP delivering legal work. Peterson expects smaller and midsized law firms to have particular difficulty hiring transition expertise. Larger legal-information businesses face demand for clean datasets, while specialized platform vendors may face competition from increasingly capable general-purpose models. The source does not quantify employment losses or changes to law-firm staffing ratios.
